toc.title: What happened in everyone's nervous systems

blocks.p: I want to share a story about neuroception that happened to my family and me recently: someone banging on our window at around 11:00 at night. I think it's a really good example of neuroception.

A few days ago, on a Saturday night, someone apparently banged on my office window. At least that's the image my wife and the kids in the house had in their minds to explain what was happening. Ours were home, and there were two friends sleeping over.

And I believe them. Afterward, once we were safe, I went outside and banged on a couple of different windows with my fists, without breaking them. And they said, "Yes, that's what we heard," except louder. I was asleep when the noise happened, so I did not directly hear it. I'll come back to that when I talk about neuroception.

To add more evidence to what happened, they noticed that the light above the garage door came on, and that only comes on if there's movement. So we're assuming someone banged on the window and then ran across the lawn past the garage, which set off the motion sensor.
Let me break this down in terms of the initial autonomic response, and then connect it to neuroception.

We had family friends over that day for a pool party. It was super hot. The kids were swimming, I was in the pool, I did a lot of swimming and a lot of socializing. Those are two things that completely drain me. So by about 9:30, I was done. The other parents had gone home. I was exhausted, and I fell asleep quick.

The next thing I know, I'm out of bed and running down the hallway toward my front door. That's my recollection of that moment. I fell asleep, and all of a sudden, boom, I'm jumping out of bed and running down the hallway. My wife said something to me as I was running; I'm not quite sure what it was. The kids were freaking out in the front room. One of our dogs, who has a really deep, mean bark, was barking his head off.

I got to the front door, looked out the windows, and checked the security cameras. The kids explained what they heard, and they all said the same thing: someone was banging on a window. And they each pointed toward my office.

When I got to the door, I didn't run outside. There was an impulse to go and find whoever had done this, and I held back on it. In my neighborhood we get these Ring alerts where people share that ne'er-do-wells are trying to lure people out of the house, so someone else can jump out of the bushes and run in the house, or accost them in some form. I didn't want to open the door and open my family up to that.
My wife called the police. They came in about five minutes, walked through the neighborhood, and gave us some tips on how to make the home more secure, including getting more lighting.

blocks.h: What happened in everyone's nervous systems

blocks.p: So let's get back to what happened in our nervous systems at the moment of that banging noise.

The kids mobilized enough to group together in the living room. The girls were up a little later watching TV in the living room, and the boys were trying to sleep in my son's bedroom. After the banging, my daughter said she kind of froze for a moment and then yelled, "Hey." She laughed about it, because it's all that came out of her mouth. But she yelled it with enough sympathetic activation that it alerted my wife, who I think was already up. And it may have helped wake me up.

I don't know what woke me up. It might have been my daughter yelling, my wife jumping out of bed, my wife saying something to me, the dog barking, or the sound on the window itself. It might have been all of those things.

For me, I mobilized really quickly, and without a second thought. Now, is that because I'm the man of the house protecting my family? Is it because I'm brave and ready to take on any intruders? Possibly. But also, maybe kind of not. Let's talk about neuroception to get into that a little deeper.

If you don't know the Polyvagal Theory, neuroception is the body's unconscious detection of information from the internal and external world. For the external world, it uses your five senses to detect safety and danger in the environment. That information gets sent to the brainstem, and the brainstem shifts the body's processes to adapt to the needs of the present moment, the needs of survival.

It could shift the body into a state of safety and social connection. It could shift the body into mobilization, flight or fight. Or it could shift it into immobilization, shutdown. It's more complex than that, but those are the three basic primary states.
The key points to know here: neuroception is unconscious, and neuroception triggers these state shifts based on the needs for survival.

So, back to how I responded. I mobilized without a second thought. That's true. But I also never had a first thought. I never made a conscious decision to wake up. I never decided to get out of bed and go to the front of the house. I never thought, "I'm going to protect my loved ones and my home." I just did the actions I did. My body mobilized. I didn't choose it. It just happened.

So I wouldn't say I was brave. I didn't feel fear. I didn't feel hesitation. It's not like I had to will myself through it despite feeling fear. I actually didn't feel anything at all. It was a moment of pure impulsive movement, driven by my sympathetic mobility instincts, as best I can tell.

I went from being shut down and unconscious, asleep, to mobilized and alert. I wouldn't say I was conscious, at least not right off the bat. But I was alert. My body was responding to the external cues of danger. I was taking in the information, but not consciously processing it and thinking about it. I was just neurocepting and then reacting. There was no initial thought process about what to do next.

By the time I got to the door, I was more awake, more conscious. I was trying to piece together what had happened from everyone's reports, and I was conscious enough not to open the front door in case there was some sort of elaborate ruse to get in the house.

To give you an idea of how fast this unconscious mobilization happened, here's how my wife described it: "You levitated out of bed." I promise you, I've never gotten out of bed that fast. Typically it's more deliberate, kind of a slow process. She was actually up before I was, mobilized and heading that direction, but my body just willed itself out of bed based on what it was neurocepting as dangerous.

So I neurocepted danger from the environment. Even when we're asleep, our bodies are still detecting safety and danger. I probably felt my wife's sudden mobilization in the mattress. Maybe I heard the bang in my sleep. The dog barking, the kids freaking out: all of these things indicated danger.

My brainstem accurately neurocepted danger and shifted my body into a mobilized state, probably more of an aggressive one: fight. I say that because I was going toward the danger. I wasn't evading it, escaping it, or running away. My legs carried my body toward the danger, with the biological intention of protecting family and territory.

I say biological intention because I think that's an instinct that's part of us: to protect our home territory and our loved ones. This was a purely biological process. I'd love to say I was super brave and protected everybody, but really, there was absolutely no choice in the matter. My body did it without my conscious direction or will.

We're safe. The sleepover ended; we called the other kids' parents and they came and got them. I ended up sleeping on the couch, and my kids went to our bed. I slept a little, and when I did, I pretty much had one eye open. It was a terrible night of sleep.

The next day we bought a Ring camera and set it up where the noise came from, which was the darkest part of our front yard. We put up motion sensor spotlights, and we're going to add some permanent lights that stay on all night as well. We've taken some measures to make something like this less likely to happen again. Hopefully it doesn't. It was a pretty rough night for everybody.
